source: Fleming (2001) Recombinant uncertainty in technological search
finding: Founding data. Familiar components raise the mean citations of a patent. Reusing a familiar combination raises the mean and cuts the spread. Cumulative reuse of the same combination lowers the mean.
numbers: All US patents granted May and June 1990, n=17,264. Negative binomial models of citations. Component familiarity: +147% expected citations at max (2.28) vs min; +11.3% per 1 SD. Combination familiarity: +332% at max (11.25) vs 0; +10.3% per 1 SD. Cumulative combination use: at max 26.76 a patent gets 37.9% of the citations it would get at 0; -5.6% per 1 SD.
quote: the models cannot convincingly reject the alternative argument that the results merely reflect the normal life-cycle progression
limits: One cross-section, two months, one country. Citations are a proxy for usefulness. Author says the models cannot separate learning from technology life-cycle effects or popularity. Author's own half-sample splits kept signs but not always significance.
agent_relevance: O7: familiar pieces raise the average result. Do not keep re-using the same analogue pair.

source: Fleming (2001) Recombinant uncertainty in technological search (hypothesis 2, spread)
finding: Failed prediction inside the founding paper. Component learning was predicted to cut the spread of outcomes. It did not, in a simple way. The effect is U-shaped: familiar components cut spread a little, then very familiar components raise it.
numbers: Hypothesis 2 not supported. Largest spread reduction is 9.6% at the 60th percentile of component familiarity (variance 25.32 vs 28.02 at mean citations 3.80). The effect turns positive at the 96th percentile. Combination familiarity cuts spread: 2.2% at the mean, 64% at the max (hypothesis 4 supported).
limits: A 9.6% reduction is small. Fleming reads the positive tail as inventors taking more risk with extremely familiar parts, in line with Utterback's claim that radical innovation uses well-known components.
agent_relevance: The rule 'familiar pieces are safe' is not monotone. Very familiar pieces joined in a new way are still risky. Keep a spread-aware check at the extremes.

source: Fleming (2001), how 'new combination' was measured
finding: The headline 'new combinations have lower mean and higher variance' is tested through combination familiarity (prior reuse count), not by an experiment on novel pairs. A new combination is one with low prior use.
numbers: Mean combination familiarity is 0.28, so most patents are near-new. Positive significant effect on the mean and negative significant effect on dispersion in Models 2 and 3.
limits: The pdftotext table layout is garbled, so exact coefficient placement was not trusted and none are quoted. Recheck against the journal PDF before citing coefficients.
agent_relevance: Counting how often a mapping was used before measures the same thing: low prior use predicts a lower mean and a wider spread.

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact (Science 342:468)
finding: Best science-side support. Impact peaks for papers that are mostly conventional in their reference combinations and add a small tail of unusual ones. Novelty alone is not enough.
numbers: 17.9 million Web of Science papers, 15,613 journals. Hit = top 5% of citations (8-year). High median conventionality + high tail novelty: 9.11 hits per 100 (about 1.8x the 5% base rate). Conventional only: 5.82. Novel tail only: 5.33. Neither: 2.05. Shares of papers: 6.7%, 23%, 26%, 44%. Only 3.54% (1980s) and 2.67% (1990s) of papers have median z below 0; about 41% have an atypical tail. Peak impact at the 85th to 95th percentile of median conventionality.
quote: papers that mix high tail novelty with high median conventionality have nearly twice the propensity to be unusually highly cited
limits: Journal-pair z-scores as the combination unit. Observational. Later shown to track interdisciplinarity (Fontana 2020).
agent_relevance: O7: a far analogue should sit inside an otherwise conventional problem frame. One distant source plus mostly standard moves beats all-distant or all-standard.

source: Uzzi et al. (2013), moderator: team size
finding: Teams add unusual combinations without giving up the conventional core. The advantage of tail novelty holds at any conventionality level and any authorship structure.
numbers: Teams are 37.7% more likely than solo authors to insert novel combinations into familiar domains. Tail novelty in 36.2% of solo papers, 39.9% of two-author papers, 49.7% of papers with three or more authors.
limits: Association only. Authors choose their teams.
agent_relevance: Several independent draws plus a checker may play the role teams play here (G3, G5).

source: Wang, Veugelers, Stephan (2017) Bias against novelty in science (NBER w22180; Research Policy 46:1416)
finding: Mean and spread both hold at paper level. Novel papers (first-time journal pairs in the reference list) have a wider citation spread, fatter top and bottom tails and more big hits, but are recognised late.
numbers: All 2001 Web of Science articles, 1,056,936 field-article observations. 89% make no new journal pair; 11% do; 55% of those make one. Highly novel vs non-novel: odds of top 10% cited +16.80%, odds of bottom 10% +16.76% (both tails up). Odds of a top 1% big hit +39.82% (highly novel), +11.22% (moderately novel). Cited by big hits +26.20%.
quote: No prophet is accepted in his own country.
limits: Journal-pair novelty only; field dependent. Observational.
agent_relevance: A rewarded wide spread is real: novelty buys upside and downside together. O7 should stay out of routine problems.

source: Wang et al. (2017), moderators: citation window and home vs foreign field
finding: Window length flips the sign of the novelty effect. Home field versus foreign field flips it again.
numbers: Highly novel papers are less likely to be top cited with windows under 3 years; significantly more likely from year 4, gap growing with window. Moderately novel papers need windows of 9+ years. Cited by 16.56% (high) and 10.05% (moderate) more subject categories. Top 1% in foreign fields: odds +62.37% (highly novel), +29.39% (moderate). In the home field: not significant for highly novel, -8.37% for moderately novel.
limits: Same 2001 dataset. Windows tested only to 14 years.
agent_relevance: A judge that grades a new mapping right after generation, inside its own frame, will undervalue novel mappings. Use a delayed or outside-frame check.

source: Wang et al. (2017), skew of the novelty measure
finding: Novelty is rare and heavy-tailed. A notable paper can be highly novel and still not be top cited.
numbers: Denk and Horstmann paper scored 8.9891 (top 1% novel) but was not top 1% cited in its subject category. Social sciences, especially psychology, score above most fields; physical sciences, especially space sciences and physics, score low.
limits: Field-dependent measure.
agent_relevance: Most mapping trials will be low-novelty ones; budget a few draws at the tail, not many.

source: Lee, Walsh, Wang (2015) Creativity in scientific teams: unpacking novelty and impact (Research Policy 44:684)
finding: Novelty and impact come from different processes. Team size has an inverted-U link to novelty, driven by field and task variety. Team size has a steadily rising link to high-impact status. Variety has no direct effect on impact once novelty is controlled.
numbers: Survey of papers from 2001-2006 stratified by 22 fields with oversampling of the top 1% cited; 9,428 sampled papers, 2,327 completed responses (26% response rate), about 1,245 observations in the models.
limits: Survey nonresponse. Reference-pair measure. The squared terms of two alternative size measures (log headcount, log funds) were not significant.
agent_relevance: Gaining novelty (variety) and gaining reach (more draws, more reviewers) are separate dials.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can recombination growth lead to scientific breakthroughs? (arXiv 2402.16839)
finding: Rival theory. More atypical references go with LOWER disruption, in all fields, periods and team sizes. In a quasi-experiment on preprint versions, adding atypical references to the same paper lowered disruption.
numbers: 18,931,951 papers 1900-2010 in Figure 2 (abstract says 19 million). 2,461 papers with early and later versions: change in disruption on change in atypicality, coefficient -0.0009, p<0.05.
limits: Disruption (D index) is a different outcome from citation hits. The version comparison is observational. The effect is small.
agent_relevance: If the aim is to displace a default answer, adding far analogues may not help. Aim the mapping at the rival structure.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2024), 20 surveyed breakthroughs
finding: Case evidence for displacement. Disruptive breakthroughs line up with one or few specific predecessor ideas they were built to replace, rather than a broad recombination.
numbers: Surveyed scientists nominated 3 to 10 disruptive papers each; the 20 most disruptive had mean D-score 0.21 (top 2%).
limits: Small expert-nominated sample.
agent_relevance: A good O7 mapping may target a specific rival structure rather than maximise distance.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can recombination displace dominant scientific ideas? (arXiv 2506.15959)
finding: Larger version of the contrast. Atypicality marks work that extends known ideas into new topics. Disruption marks replacement of a dominant idea in its own topic. They are different processes and negatively related.
numbers: 40,935,251 articles 1965-2020 in Figure 3 (41 million 1965-2024 in the abstract). Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct zero-shot labelled 50,147 highly cited disruptive papers as theory or method advances relative to the top reference; the theory probability falls as the time gap to that reference grows.
limits: The LLM labels were not validated against humans in the text read. Correlation only. Uses the same atypicality measure Fontana 2020 doubts.
agent_relevance: An LLM could label whether a mapping changes the concept or only refines it, as a cheap check.

source: Fontana, Iori, Montobbio, Sinatra (2020) New and atypical combinations (Research Policy 49:104063)
finding: Weakened validation. Tested against Nobel-related and APS Milestone articles with a configuration null model. First-appearance novelty mostly reflects citation-network structure and does not separate novel from non-novel articles. Atypical-combination novelty overlaps with interdisciplinarity. Authors say policy built on these indicators should be reassessed.
numbers: 230,854 articles from 8 American Physical Society journals, 1985-2005; 2.4 million citations.
limits: Only the publisher summary page was read, not the full paper. No Nobel counts or correlations were on that page.
agent_relevance: The Uzzi and Wang measures may not measure novelty. Treat the 'distant combination helps' evidence as weaker than the headline numbers.

source: Bornmann, Tekles, Zhang, Ye (2019) Do we measure novelty when we analyze unusual combinations of cited references? (J. Informetrics)
finding: Convergent validity test of two reference-based novelty scores against expert tags in F1000Prime. Score U (Uzzi-style) mostly behaves as expected. Score W (Wang-style) mostly does not.
numbers: Papers from 2013-2015. Detailed model n=23,206 papers, pseudo R2 0.33%. One SD rise in U gives +7.47% expected 'new finding' tags.
limits: Biomedicine only. Expert tags are noisy. Very low explanatory power despite significance.
agent_relevance: If bibliometric 'novelty' barely tracks expert judgement, LLM novelty ratings are also unvalidated. Use blind held-out outcomes (G5, G8).

source: Ke, Teng, Min (2024) Relying on recent and temporally dispersed science predicts breakthrough inventions (arXiv 2107.09176 v2)
finding: Boundary condition on reuse. Search in science raises patent impact. The useful kind is recent plus age-varied sources. Low age variance offsets the benefit.
numbers: 3,693,101 US patents, 1976-2009. Only 12.5% cite scientific papers. Those patents get +49% 10-year citations and +117% odds of being a top-5% hit. Technological search adds +39% citations alone, +84% with science search. Top-5% hit probability 2.3% to 4.8% when science refs are added. Above-average recency: +14% citations, +25% hit odds. Above-average age variance: +16% citations, +32% hit odds.
limits: Observational; patents that cite science differ in many ways. Citations only.
agent_relevance: Mix source freshness and source variety. Do not draw all analogues from one era or field.

source: Ke et al. (2024), robustness across thresholds
finding: Results hold across hit thresholds and technology fields. The joint effect is larger than each search alone and bigger further up the tail.
numbers: Odds of a top-1% hit rise 171%, versus 117% (top 5%) and 96% (top 10%). With science search the technological search effect is a 144% rise in hit probability vs 68% without.
limits: Citation counts only; small share of patents has science references.
agent_relevance: Combining two search spaces beats each alone.

source: Mukherjee, Romero, Jones, Uzzi (2017) The nearly universal link between the age of past knowledge and tomorrow's breakthroughs (Science Advances 3:e1601315)
finding: Stable across fields. Works citing mostly recent knowledge with a wide spread of ages are about twice as likely to be top-5% cited. Other age mixes do no better than chance.
numbers: 28,426,345 Web of Science papers (1945-2013) and 5,382,833 US patents (1950-2010). Hotspot papers are 2.2 times as likely to be top 5%; 75% of papers lie outside the hotspot. Fields showing the link rose from about 60% (postwar) to about 90% (2000s).
limits: Citations as impact. Age is a proxy for knowledge use.
agent_relevance: Do not make every source the same age. A recent core with some old sources was the pattern that held.

source: Verhoeven, Bakker, Veugelers (2016) Measuring technological novelty with patent-based indicators (Research Policy 45:707)
finding: Three kinds of novelty (new recombination NR, new technological origins NTO, new scientific origins NSO) raise the chance of outliers, most when they co-occur. All three together is rare.
numbers: Patent families from PATSTAT. About 25% score on at least one indicator; under 1% (15,339) on all three. 2-SD outlier base rate is 3.3%; observed over expected: 1.86 (any), 1.87 (NTO), 2.11 (NR), 3.82 (NSO), 6.48 (all three). 22% of all-three patents are 2-SD outliers. At 5 SD: 15.39x expected, 8% of all-three patents. At 10 SD: 28x.
limits: Contingency tables, not causal. Novel patents also reach the low tail (higher variance).
agent_relevance: Plan for a wider spread, not a higher mean. Few draws should be extreme.

source: Verhoeven et al. (2016), spread claim
finding: Supports the variance half of Fleming. Technological novelty raises the spread of citation impact. The abstract states this for most novelty cases.
numbers: Every novelty category had a higher chance than 3.3% of landing among +2 SD outliers.
limits: The mean effect is not what this paper tests.
agent_relevance: Judge a far-analogue policy by its top-of-distribution yield, not by its mean.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky, Evans (2015) Tradition and innovation in scientists' research strategies (Am. Sociol. Rev. 80:875)
finding: Sharpest negative on expected value. Rare, risky strategies earn more citations on average and have a wider spread, but the extra reward does not cover the extra risk of going unpublished or ignored.
numbers: 6,455,756 MEDLINE abstracts (1934-2008) with 2+ chemicals. Surprisal explains 29.2% of variation in mean citations (F(1,98)=30.96) and 28.6% of variation in the SD of citations. A strategy ten times less probable gets 2.26 extra citations. Prize winners (137 prizes) use more jump strategies.
limits: Biomedical chemistry only. Unpublished work is not in citations.
agent_relevance: A far analogue is worth it only where an upside is needed (impasse or open mode).

source: Foster et al. (2015), stability of strategy mix
finding: Competing explanation for why novel combinations are rare. The strategy mix stayed stable over 1983-2008 while knowledge grew, and the fitted model shows a rising preference for repeating known links.
numbers: Model prediction vs observation Pearson R=0.983. Repeat links dominate; jumps are the rarest.
limits: Single abstract-agent model; not a causal test.
agent_relevance: The pull toward the familiar is strong. LLM samples also repeat (see KOMBINE), so explicit nudges may be needed.

source: Kaplan, Vakili (2015) The double-edged sword of recombination in breakthrough innovation (SMJ 36:1435)
finding: Rival result. Patents that open a new topic come more from local search, not distant search. Economic value comes from broad recombination plus novelty. Novelty and usefulness have different search origins.
numbers: Abstract page only. Nanotechnology patents with a topic-model novelty measure. Sample given as 2,826 in the abstract and 2,384 in a later review; sources disagree.
quote: economic value is the product of broader recombinations as well as novelty
limits: Abstract only. Different novelty measure, so not comparable with citation-pair measures.
agent_relevance: Local depth can produce the idea; breadth gets it valued. Use local search for the idea, far analogues for the framing.

source: Singh, Fleming (2010) Lone inventors as sources of breakthroughs (Management Science 56:41)
finding: Refines the variance story. Collaboration cuts very poor outcomes and raises extreme successes at once, so the spread is not a symmetric widening. Lone inventors are less likely to hit breakthroughs and more likely to produce very poor results.
numbers: Over half a million patented inventions, per a search summary. Quantile regressions.
limits: Not opened this session; from a search summary only.
agent_relevance: A second reader can remove the bad tail without removing the good one. Supports separating generator from judge (G5, G8).

source: Kneeland, Schilling, Aharonson (2020) Exploring uncharted territory: outlier innovation (Organization Science 31:535)
finding: Outlier patents tend to come from long search paths, scientific reasoning and distant recombination. Exploratory analysis plus inventor interviews.
numbers: No numbers read this session.
limits: Not opened. Exploratory; US outlier patents only.
agent_relevance: Outlier outcomes need a long path, not one jump.

source: Schilling, Green (2011) Recombinant search and breakthrough idea generation (Research Policy 40:1321)
finding: Matched-sample test on social science papers. High-impact papers show wider and deeper search and atypical cross-domain links, after controlling for author experience.
numbers: No numbers read this session.
limits: Not opened. Later work (Fontana 2020) found such indicators weakly linked to recognised breakthroughs.
agent_relevance: Consistent with the Uzzi pattern; weak evidence.

source: Combinatorial Creativity / KOMBINE benchmark (arXiv 2509.21043)
finding: LLMs find a shared abstraction far less often than they find associations. Once found, the blend is almost always coherent. Different models converge on the same invented concepts.
numbers: 35 LLMs and 75 retained humans (of 120). Factual association 59.0%, valid analogy 53.4%, valid blend 43.4%. Given a valid generic space, coherent blend 97.1%. 2,070 invented concepts, 7,868 properties; 19.9% (412) reuse two or more properties of another model's concept; blends 37.3% vs analogies 2.6%. Same-provider pairs share more (9.3% vs 4.1%). Humans: association 22.1%, analogy 32.9%, blend 12.8%. Association originality correlates with valid blends r=0.48 (p=0.003).
quote: models can find a generic space only 43.4% of the time on average
limits: Constructed items, not open research. Page read to 100,000 of 183,325 characters.
agent_relevance: O7 needs an explicit abstraction step with a typed mapping. Samples from one model family converge, so spread must come from different prompts or sources.
